ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In a game of Chomp, two players alternately take bites from a 5-by-7 grid of unit squares. To take a bite, a player chooses one of the remaining squares, then removes ("eats'') all squares in the quadrant defined by the left edge (extended upward) and the lower edge (extended rightward) of the chosen square. For example, the bite determined by the shaded square in the diagram would remove the shaded square and the four squares marked by $\times$. (The squares with two or more dotted edges have been removed form the original board in previous moves.)
<image1>

The object of the game is to make one's opponent take the last bite. The diagram shows one of the many subsets of the set of 35 unit squares that can occur during the game of Chomp. How many different subsets are there in all? Include the full board and empty board in your count.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a rectangular unit-square chessboard with 5 rows and 7 columns. In the upper right there are several squares already removed, indicated by dashed boundaries; a gray shaded square is located slightly left of the middle of the chessboard; among several still relevant squares in the same column upward from this shaded square and in the upper-right direction, four squares are marked with X, indicating that if the shaded square is selected as the position of this bite, the shaded square and these X squares will be removed at the same time. This image example conforms to the meaning of the problem: one bite will remove the upper-right quadrant part of the selected square. Reasoning: Because each bite removes some remaining square and all related remaining squares above and to its right, any remaining set that can appear must be lower-left closed: if some square is still there, then the squares to its left and below must also still be there; otherwise, if those lower-left squares had once been bitten off, this square would also have been bitten off together with them. Conversely, any lower-left closed shape can be obtained by successively biting off the boundary squares of its complement, so the subsets that can appear are exactly the lower-left closed staircase shapes in the 5×7 rectangle. Such a staircase shape is uniquely determined by a monotone boundary path from the upper-left side of the rectangle to the lower-right side. The path needs 5 vertical steps and 7 horizontal steps in total, in any order. Therefore the number is C(12,5)=C(12,7)=792. This count includes the extreme boundary paths corresponding to the complete chessboard and the empty chessboard.

method.method_draft: Use a monotone boundary-path model. First read the image: the board is a 5-row by 7-column rectangle, and the example bite from the shaded square removes that square together with squares above and to the right of it, matching the marked X squares and the dotted previously removed upper-right region. From the text, bites always remove such upper-right quadrants. Therefore any reachable set of remaining squares must be a lower-left-justified shape: if a square remains, every square weakly below and weakly to its left must also remain. Conversely, any such lower-left-justified shape can be produced by removing the complementary upper-right region through suitable bites. Such a shape is determined by its staircase-like boundary from the upper-left side to the lower-right side of the 5-by-7 rectangle. The boundary consists of 5 vertical steps and 7 horizontal steps in some order, so the number of possible subsets is the number of such paths, namely binomial(12,5)=binomial(12,7)=792, including the all-full and all-empty boundary extremes.

method.method_draft: Use row-length sequences. From the image, observe that in any displayed reachable position, each row of remaining squares begins at the left edge, and lower rows are at least as long as rows above them; the dotted removed squares occur only in upper-right portions. From the text, each bite removes all squares above/right of a chosen square, so this row-length monotonicity is preserved after every move. Let the remaining row lengths from bottom to top be r1,r2,r3,r4,r5. Then each ri is an integer between 0 and 7, and the condition for a valid reachable subset is 7 >= r1 >= r2 >= r3 >= r4 >= r5 >= 0. Conversely, any weakly decreasing 5-tuple in this range represents a valid Chomp position. Thus the count is the number of multisets of size 5 chosen from the 8 possible row lengths 0,1,...,7, which is C(8+5-1,5)=C(12,5)=792.

ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In a game of Chomp, two players alternately take bites from a 5-by-7 grid of unit squares. To take a bite, a player chooses one of the remaining squares, then removes ("eats") all squares in the quadrant defined by the left edge (extended upward) and the lower edge (extended rightward) of the chosen square. For example, the bite determined by the shaded square in the diagram would remove the shaded square and the four squares marked by $\times$. (The squares with two or more dotted edges have been removed from the original board in previous moves.) The object of the game is to make one's opponent take the last bite. The diagram shows one of the many subsets of the set of 35 unit squares that can occur during the game of Chomp. How many different subsets are there in all? Include the full board and empty board in your count.
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The figure is a rectangular unit-square chessboard with 5 rows and 7 columns. In the upper right there are several squares already removed, indicated by dashed boundaries; a gray shaded square is located slightly left of the middle of the chessboard; among several still relevant squares in the same column upward from this shaded square and in the upper-right direction, four squares are marked with X, indicating that if the shaded square is selected as the position of this bite, the shaded square and these X squares will be removed at the same time. This image example conforms to the meaning of the problem: one bite will remove the upper-right quadrant part of the selected square.
Reasoning: Because each bite removes some remaining square and all related remaining squares above and to its right, any remaining set that can appear must be lower-left closed: if some square is still there, then the squares to its left and below must also still be there; otherwise, if those lower-left squares had once been bitten off, this square would also have been bitten off together with them. Conversely, any lower-left closed shape can be obtained by successively biting off the boundary squares of its complement, so the subsets that can appear are exactly the lower-left closed staircase shapes in the 5×7 rectangle.
Such a staircase shape is uniquely determined by a monotone boundary path from the upper-left side of the rectangle to the lower-right side. The path needs 5 vertical steps and 7 horizontal steps in total, in any order. Therefore the number is C(12,5)=C(12,7)=792. This count includes the extreme boundary paths corresponding to the complete chessboard and the empty chessboard.
